metadata.scope: e_scandinavia (all baronies across k_denmark, k_finland, k_norway, k_sapmi, and k_sweden)

schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if not extracted from retrieved summary and flagged for manual check).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 AD start date; false if anachronistic or unattested <= 867 (candidate for Step 2 resolution).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty/settler after 867 AD.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 AD exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier). Every exists=true entry carries first_mention_year <= 867.

b_aalborg.first_mention_attestation: Coins minted under King Harthacnut (c. 1040 CE), inscribed 'Alabu' / 'Alabur'.
b_aalborg.etymology_analysis: Attested c. 1040 CE as 'Alabu' ('Alabur'), combining Old Norse 'ál' (narrow stream or channel, referring to the Limfjord narrows or Østerå) with 'bú' (dwelling/settlement), later replaced by 'borg' (fortress, town).

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

older_name_by_867.notes: Archaeological remains exist in the Limfjord area (such as Lindholm Høje, a separate barony), but no distinct older name for Aalborg itself is attested on or before 867 CE.

b_lindholm.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological settlement at Lindholm Høje dates from c. 400–1200 CE; the toponym 'Lindholm' is not attested on or before 867 CE and first appears in late medieval records.

morphemes.translation: islet, elevated dry ground in marshland

b_lindholm.etymology_analysis: From Old Danish 'lind' (lime/linden tree) and 'holm' (islet or dry elevation surrounded by wetland), referring to the elevated ridge north of the Limfjord.

older_name_by_867.notes: Although Lindholm Høje was a major Iron Age and Viking Age burial and settlement site, no written name for it is attested on or before 867 CE.

b_randros.first_mention_attestation: Coins minted under King Canute the Holy (1080–1086 CE), inscribed 'Ranrosia' and 'Randrusia'.
b_randros.etymology_analysis: Compounded from Old Danish 'rand' (ridge, hillside) and 'áróss' (river mouth), meaning 'the hillside by the river mouth' (Gudenå at Randers Fjord). Early forms include 'Ranrosia' (c. 1086 CE) and 'Randrøs' (1231 CE), evolving into modern 'Randers'.

b_aarhus.first_mention_attestation: Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum, recording Bishop Reginbrand of 'Aros' at the Synod of Ingelheim in 948 CE.
b_aarhus.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse 'Áróss' (Old Danish 'Arus'), meaning 'mouth of the river' (Aarhus Å). Later folk-etymologically reshaped with '-hus' ('house') to 'Aarhus' (first attested in 1406 CE).

older_name_by_867.notes: Archaeology shows coastal settlement from the 8th century CE, but the name 'Aros' is first attested in 948 CE.

b_jelling.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century Danish sources (earlier royal center of Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth c. 955–965 CE, though the Jelling runestones do not record the place name).
b_jelling.etymology_analysis: From Old Danish '*Jalung', an '-ung' derivative of a reconstructed color adjective '*jal' ('yellow', cognate with Old High German 'elo'), meaning 'the yellow place' (referring to soil or vegetation).

b_djursland.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 1200 CE as 'Dyursa' (river name) and in medieval sources as 'Diursland'.
b_djursland.etymology_analysis: Means 'the land around Diursa', where 'Diursa' (attested c. 1200 CE as 'Dyursa', an older name for the Grenaa river) means 'the river where many deer/animals gather'.

b_ringkobing.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1340 CE as 'Rennumkøpingh' (later 'Rænnumkøpingh' in 1345 CE and 'Rennekøping' in 1368 CE).
b_ringkobing.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby older parish village of Rindum (Old Danish 'Rænnum') combined with 'køping' ('market town'), attested in 1340 CE as 'Rennumkøpingh'.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_holstebro.first_mention_attestation: Letter issued by Bishop Tyge of Ribe on 6 February 1274 CE, as 'Holstatbro'.

morphemes.translation: hollow place / fortified ford or homestead

b_holstebro.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1274 CE as 'Holstatbro', referring to a bridge ('bro') over the Storåen river at a hollow or settlement site ('holstat').

b_ycost.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1310 CE as 'Ykost' (and 1340 CE as 'Ycost'), modern Ikast.
b_ycost.etymology_analysis: Older attested form of Ikast (1310 CE 'Ykost', 1340 CE 'Ycost'), from Old Danish '*i' ('yew') and 'kost' ('thicket/scrub'), meaning 'yew thicket'.

morphemes.translation: intestine, used metaphorically for a long narrow strip of land

b_tarm.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1347 CE as 'Thaarm', from Old Danish 'tarm' used topographically for a long, narrow ridge or strip of terrain near the Skjern Å ford.

b_viborg.first_mention_attestation: Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (c. 1075 CE); later 'Vvibiærgh' in King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE).
b_viborg.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse 'Vébjǫrg' / Old Danish 'Vvibiærgh', meaning 'sanctuary on the hill' ('vé' sacred site + 'bjerg' hill), with the second element later reshaped to 'borg' ('fortress').

older_name_by_867.notes: Viking settlement dates to the late 8th century CE, but the name is not attested on or before 867 CE.

b_ormstrup.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1354 CE as the ancestral seat of the Hvas family (and recorded prior to 1371 CE).
b_ormstrup.eponym_details: Orm (an Old Danish personal name; unattested individual, not a documented post-867 historical figure).
b_ormstrup.etymology_analysis: Manor in Sahl Sogn near Viborg, compounded from the Old Danish personal name 'Orm' and '-torp' ('outlying settlement/farmstead'), first attested in 1354 CE.

b_odense.first_mention_attestation: Imperial charter of Otto III dated 18 March 988 CE, granting privileges to the bishopric of 'Othenesuuig'.
b_odense.eponym_details: Odin (Old Norse: Óðinn), the Norse god.
b_odense.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse 'Óðins vé' ('Odin's sanctuary'), attested in 988 CE in Latinized form as 'Othenesuuig'.

older_name_by_867.notes: Archaeological evidence shows proto-urban activity from the late 8th century CE, but no name is attested on or before 867 CE.

b_svendborg.first_mention_attestation: Deed of gift by King Valdemar II in 1229 CE, naming the fortification 'Swinæburgh'.

morphemes.translation: swine, pig (or porpoise in the sound)

b_svendborg.etymology_analysis: First recorded in 1229 CE as 'Swinæburgh', from Old Danish 'svin' ('pig' or 'porpoise') and 'borg' ('fortification'), later folk-etymologically associated with the personal name Svend.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Svendborgsund sound and strait of Funen (in-game: Svendborg)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1229 Danish royal castle fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Svendborgsund sound.

b_middelfart.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Mæthælfar'.
b_middelfart.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE as 'Mæthælfar' in King Valdemar's Census Book, from Old Danish 'mæthal' ('middle') and 'far' ('passage/crossing'), referring to the middle crossing over the Little Belt.

b_nykobing.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Nykoping'.
b_nykobing.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE as 'Nykoping', meaning 'new market town', referring to Nykøbing on the island of Falster.

b_nakskov.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Nacascogh'.
b_nakskov.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE as 'Nacascogh', combining Old Danish 'nakke' (ridge/headland) or a related personal/terrain name with 'skov' ('forest/woods').

b_roskilde.first_mention_attestation: Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (c. 1075 CE, as 'Roschilde'; coins minted under King Cnut c. 1020s).
b_roskilde.eponym_details: Ro / Hróarr (legendary king/founder in medieval Danish tradition, though linguists also debate Old Norse 'hross' [horse] or personal name *Ro).
b_roskilde.etymology_analysis: Traditionally explained as 'Ro's spring' (after legendary founder King Ro/Hróarr + Old Danish 'kilde' [spring]), attested in the 11th century CE on coins and in Adam of Bremen ('Roschilde').

current_repo_state.b_origin: Roskilde — Historical Option A seat of c_sjaelland

b_helsingora.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Helsingør'.
b_helsingora.eponym_details: Helsingar (inhabitants of the 'hals', i.e., the narrow neck of the Øresund strait).

morphemes.translation: dweller by the narrow strait (from hals, 'neck')

b_helsingora.etymology_analysis: First mentioned in 1231 CE in King Valdemar's Census Book; derived from 'helsing' (people living at the 'hals' or narrow strait of the Øresund) and 'ør' ('gravelly shore').

b_hafn.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1043 CE as 'Hafnæ' (modern Danish 'Havn'); later in the 12th century as 'Købmannahavn' / 'Portus Mercatorum'.
b_hafn.etymology_analysis: Old Danish 'Hafn' ('harbor', attested 1043 CE as 'Hafnæ'), the original short name of Copenhagen before it was expanded to 'Købmannahavn' ('merchants' harbor') in the 12th century CE.

b_naestved.first_mention_attestation: Foundation charter of St. Peter's Benedictine Monastery in Næstved (1135 CE) by Peder Bodilsen.
b_naestved.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1135 CE, from Old Danish 'næs' ('headland') and 'tved' ('woodland clearing'), referring to a cleared settlement on a promontory near the Suså river.

b_slagelse.first_mention_attestation: Coins minted under King Cnut (1018–1035 CE); written form 'Slauløsæ' attested in King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE).
b_slagelse.etymology_analysis: Minting attested under Cnut (1018–1035 CE) and written 'Slauløsæ' in 1231 CE, from Old Danish 'slag' ('hollow/depression') and '-løse' ('clearing/meadow').

b_bregne.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE / c. 1300 copy), mentioning Bräkne-Hoby ('Hughby') in Bräkne hundred.
b_bregne.etymology_analysis: Danish form 'Bregne' of Swedish 'Bräkne' (Bräkne härad / Bräkne-Hoby in Blekinge), named after the Bräkneån river, from Old Danish 'bregne' ('fern/bracken').

b_ronneby.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Rotnæby'.
b_ronneby.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE as 'Rotnæby', combining the old river name 'Rotn' ('the roaring river', referring to the rapids of Ronnebyån) with 'by' ('settlement').

b_lister.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Lister'.
b_lister.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE in King Valdemar's Census Book, referring to the Listerlandet peninsula and Lister hundred in western Blekinge, derived from a root meaning 'strip/edge of land'.

older_name_by_867.notes: The 6th–7th century CE Blekinge runestones stand on Listerlandet, but they do not attest the place name 'Lister'.

b_avaskar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1350 CE as a town in eastern Blekinge.
b_avaskar.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1350 CE; combines 'ava' (shallow inlet/cove) and 'skär' (rocky skerry/islet) on the eastern Blekinge coast.

b_ronne.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1277 CE (and referred to as a market town in 1327 CE).
b_ronne.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1277 CE, located by a natural harbor on Bornholm; likely derived from Old Danish 'røn' (stony/gravelly bank or rowan).

b_halmstad.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as a royal manor ('Halmstath').
b_halmstad.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE in King Valdemar's Census Book as a Danish royal estate by the Nissan river, combining 'halm' (reeds/straw) and 'stath' ('place/landing').

b_onsala.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Halland records (13th century CE; pagan cult site of Odin dating to the late Viking Age).
b_onsala.eponym_details: Odin (Old Norse: Óðinn), the Norse god.
b_onsala.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse 'Óðins salr' ('Odin's hall'), reflecting a pre-Christian cult site dedicated to Odin on the Onsala peninsula.

b_laholm.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE; written 'Lagæholm' in 1275 CE).
b_laholm.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 13th century CE (1231 CE / 1275 CE 'Lagæholm'), meaning 'islet in the Lagan river', referring to the castle island of Lagaholm.

b_lund.first_mention_attestation: Coins minted under King Cnut (c. 1020 CE, 'Lundi'); founded archaeologically c. 990 CE.
b_lund.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse 'lundr' ('grove', possibly a sacred grove), founded around 990 CE and first attested on coins in the early 11th century CE.

b_trelleborg.etymology_analysis: First recorded in 1257 CE as 'Threlæburgh', named after a Viking-age ring fortress ('borg') on the site, with the first element meaning either 'thrall' or 'wooden palisade stave'.

b_tommerup.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1155 CE as 'Tummathorp' (modern Östra Tommarp).
b_tommerup.eponym_details: Tummi (Old Danish personal name; unattested individual, not a documented post-867 historical figure).
b_tommerup.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1155 CE as 'Tummathorp' (Danish 'Tommerup', Swedish 'Östra Tommarp'), from the Old Danish personal name 'Tummi' and '-thorp' ('outlying settlement').

b_goinge.first_mention_attestation: Deed of gift of King Canute the Holy (1085 CE), as 'Guthisbo' (later 'Gythinga hærath' in the 13th century CE).
b_goinge.eponym_details: Guthir (Old Danish personal name; unattested individual, not a documented post-867 historical figure).
b_goinge.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1085 CE as 'Guthisbo' and in the 13th century CE as 'Gythinga hærath' ('Göinge'), derived from the Old Danish personal name 'Guthir' with the inhabitant suffix '-inge'.

b_helsingborg.first_mention_attestation: Deed of gift of King Canute the Holy dated 21 May 1085 CE.
b_helsingborg.eponym_details: Helsingar (inhabitants of the 'hals', the narrow neck of the Øresund strait).

morphemes.translation: dweller by the narrow strait (from hals, 'neck')

b_helsingborg.etymology_analysis: First attested on 21 May 1085 CE, meaning 'fortress of the Helsingar' (the people living along the narrow neck, 'hals', of the Øresund strait).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Öresund strait and coastal sound of the Helsingar (in-game: Helsingborg)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1085 Danish royal fortress fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient sound hydronym.

b_ribe.first_mention_attestation: Rimbert's Vita Anskarii (c. 860 CE), recording King Horik II's grant of land in 'Ripa' for Ansgar's church.
b_ribe.etymology_analysis: Founded c. 705–710 CE and first attested in writing c. 860 CE as 'Ripa' in Rimbert's Vita Anskarii; derived from a Germanic root meaning 'strip' or 'riverbank'.

b_varde.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1180s CE as 'Wartwik' and 'Warwath' (and in 1231 CE as 'Warwith').
b_varde.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 1180s CE as 'Wartwik' / 'Warwath' and in 1231 CE as 'Warwith', from Old Danish 'wara' ('outfield/common') and 'wath' ('ford' over Varde Å) or 'with' ('woods').

b_strand.first_mention_attestation: First documentary mentions of the medieval North Frisian island 'Strand' (Alt-Nordstrand) and its parishes (e.g., Hersbüll in 1198 CE).

morphemes.language: Old Danish / Old Frisian / Low German

b_strand.etymology_analysis: Medieval island of 'Strand' (later Alt-Nordstrand) in North Frisia/Schleswig, submerged in the floods of 1362 and 1634 CE; from Germanic 'strand' ('shore, coast').

b_hedeby.first_mention_attestation: Ohthere of Hålogaland's voyage account (c. 890 CE) in the Old English Orosius, as 'æt Hæðum'.
b_hedeby.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse 'Heiðabýr' ('settlement on the heath'), first attested c. 890 CE as Old English 'æt Hæðum' and on 10th-century runestones as 'Haithabu'.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Royal Frankish Annals (804 CE, as 'Sliesthorp'); Rimbert's Vita Anskarii (c. 850–865 CE, as 'Sliaswich').
older_name_by_867.notes: The Viking trading emporium on the Schlei was attested in 804 CE as 'Sliesthorp' and in the mid-9th century as 'Sliaswich' before the name 'Hedeby' ('æt Hæðum') appeared c. 890 CE.

b_aabenraa.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century historical accounts as 'Opnør' / 'Apenrade' (first mentioned in the 12th century CE).
b_aabenraa.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 12th century CE as 'Opnør' (Germanized as 'Apenrade'), from Old Danish 'open' ('open') and 'ør' ('gravelly shore/beach'), meaning 'open beach'.

b_husumbro.first_mention_attestation: 1252 CE chronicle accounts of the murder of King Abel of Denmark at 'Husembro' / 'Husumbro'.

morphemes.translation: at the houses (dative plural of hus)

b_husumbro.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1252 CE as 'Husembro' ('Husumbro', modern Husum), combining 'husum' ('at the houses', dative plural) and 'bro' ('bridge').

b_vorbasse.etymology_analysis: First attested in writing in 1340 CE as 'Worbas' (despite continuous archaeological settlement since the Iron Age). Derived from Old Danish terrain/vegetation terms.

older_name_by_867.notes: Extensive Iron Age and Viking Age settlements were excavated at Vorbasse, but no written name is attested on or before 867 CE.

b_taulov.first_mention_attestation: Medieval parish and Romanesque Taulov Church built c. 1200 CE.

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly personal name or terrain feature)

b_taulov.etymology_analysis: Medieval parish in eastern Jutland with a Romanesque church dating to c. 1200 CE; the suffix '-lov' reflects Old Danish '-lev' ('inherited estate').

b_kolding.first_mention_attestation: King Valdemar's Census Book (1231 CE), as 'Kalding'.
b_kolding.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1231 CE as 'Kalding' in King Valdemar's Census Book, originally a hydronym for the Kolding Å ('the cold river', from Old Danish 'kald').

b_turku.first_mention_attestation: 1229 CE papal bull of Pope Gregory IX (as Aboa); Swedish Åbo attested 1259 CE; possible 1154 CE map reference by al-Idrisi.

morphemes.translation: marketplace, trading post (from Old East Slavic tŭrgŭ)

b_turku.etymology_analysis: Finnish Turku derives from Old East Slavic tŭrgŭ ('market, trading place'), likely entering Finnish via Varangian trade networks or Estonian (turg). The Swedish name Åbo combines å ('river') and bo ('dwelling, settlement'), referring to the settlement at the mouth of the Aura River.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Aura river trading post / Swedish Åbo (Finnish Turku) (in-game: Abô)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_rikala.first_mention_attestation: Archaeologically attested as an Iron Age cemetery and trading site (c. 600–1200 CE), but the toponym Rikala is unattested in written sources by 867 CE (earliest surviving Halikko parish records date to 1313 CE).
b_rikala.etymology_analysis: Rikala is an Iron Age trading hub and hillfort site in Halikko. Folk tradition links the name to Finnish rikas ('rich') due to its wealth, while linguists also propose derivation from Old Swedish rike ('magnate, chieftain') with the Finnish locative suffix -la.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Iron Age hillfort and trading center of Halikko / Rikala (in-game: Rîkale)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_rauma.first_mention_attestation: 1442 CE town charter granted by Karl Knutsson Bonde in the name of King Christopher of Bavaria (though a Franciscan monastery and settlement existed slightly earlier).
b_rauma.etymology_analysis: The name Rauma derives from an old Germanic/Scandinavian loanword (cf. Old Norse straumr, Swedish ström, 'stream, current, strait'), referring to the narrow coastal strait and river mouth where the medieval trading post and 1442 CE chartered town developed.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Raumanjoki River mouth (replacing 1442 Franciscan town Rauma) (in-game: Rauma)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1442 Franciscan town Rauma fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to Raumanjoki hydronym.

b_messukyla.first_mention_attestation: 1439 CE documents mentioning Messukylä as a chapel community within Pirkkala parish.
b_messukyla.etymology_analysis: Messukylä ('Mass village', Swedish Messuby) arose in the late Middle Ages around a wooden chapel where Christian Mass was celebrated, first attested in 1439 CE. Iron Age cemeteries exist in the area, but the Christianized settlement name is post-867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Pirkkala — Historical Option A seat of c_messukyla

b_ruovesi.first_mention_attestation: 1565 CE establishment of Ruovesi parish separated from Pirkkala.
b_ruovesi.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Ruovesi, combining Finnish ruoko ('reed') and vesi ('water, lake'), meaning 'reed lake'. The parish was separated from Great Pirkkala in 1565 CE.

b_porvoo.first_mention_attestation: Early 14th century CE documents (traditionally granted town rights in 1346–1347 CE by King Magnus Eriksson, or c. 1380 CE).
b_porvoo.etymology_analysis: Finnish Porvoo is a Fennicized adaptation of Swedish Borgå ('castle river'), named after the medieval earthwork fortress (Linnamäki) beside the Porvoonjoki River.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Finnic river fortress Borgå (Porvoo) (in-game: Borchâ)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_espoo.first_mention_attestation: 1431 CE written records mentioning Espå / Espoby.
b_espoo.etymology_analysis: Finnish Espoo derives from Swedish Esbo, originally Espå / Espåå ('aspen river'), referring to the Espoonjoki River lined with aspen trees, first attested in 1431 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient coastal settlement Espoo on the Gulf of Finland (in-game: Espô)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_raseborg.first_mention_attestation: 1378 CE letter mentioning Raseborg Castle as Rasaborge.
b_raseborg.etymology_analysis: Named after Raseborg Castle (Raaseporin linna), built in the 1370s CE by Bo Jonsson Grip in Snappertuna and first attested as Rasaborge in 1378 CE. The modern municipality was formed in 2009 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient coastal bay Snappertuna (replacing 1374 Swedish castle Raseborg) (in-game: Raasepori)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1374 Swedish castle Raseborg fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to native coastal bay Snappertuna.

b_vehkalahti.first_mention_attestation: 1336 CE written documents mentioning Vehkalahti as a trading settlement.
b_vehkalahti.etymology_analysis: Vehkalahti (Swedish Veckelax) combines Finnish vehka ('bog arum, Calla palustris') and lahti ('bay'), describing a coastal bay where bog arum grew. First attested in 1336 CE.

b_ulvila.first_mention_attestation: 1311 CE ecclesiastical/historical records (bishop's church permission 1332 CE; town charter 1365 CE).
b_ulvila.eponym_details: Derived from the personal name Ulvi (from Old Norse Úlfr, 'wolf') via Swedish Ulvsby ('Ulf's village'); the eponymous Ulf is an undated medieval figure rather than a documented post-867 historical person.
b_ulvila.etymology_analysis: Ulvila (Swedish Ulvsby) combines the personal name Ulvi (Old Norse Úlfr) with the Finnish settlement suffix -la (corresponding to Swedish -by, 'village'). First attested in the early 14th century CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient trading post of Ulvila on the Kokemäenjoki (in-game: Wûlvildô)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_liinmaa.first_mention_attestation: 1395 CE written mention of Liinmaa Castle (Swedish Vreghdenborg).
b_liinmaa.eponym_details: The castle's Swedish name Vreghdenborg was named after German noble mercenary Dietrich Vieregge (Wereghede, fl. late 14th century CE), whereas the Finnish name Liinmaa ('castle land' or 'flax land') is topographic.
b_liinmaa.etymology_analysis: Liinmaa (modern Linnamaa in Eurajoki) was the site of a late 14th-century wooden and brick fortress first mentioned in 1395 CE. Its Swedish name Vreghdenborg derives from Dietrich Vieregge, while Finnish Liinmaa reflects either linnamaa ('castle land') or liinamaa ('flax land').

b_telja.first_mention_attestation: 1650 CE in Mikael Wexionius's Epitome descriptionis Sueciae, Gothiae, Fenningiae et subjectarum provinciarum.
b_telja.etymology_analysis: Teljä is a traditional name for an early medieval / late Iron Age trading post on the Kokemäenjoki River in Kokemäki, likely connected to Swedish Tälje place names. It is first documented in writing in 1650 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Iron Age trading center Teljä of Satakunta (in-game: Teljê)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Pre-867 native toponym restored over post-867 colonial foundation.

b_pirkkala.first_mention_attestation: 9 May 1374 CE document issued in Turku recording testimonies of inhabitants of Ulvila, Kokemäki, and Pirkkala (Birkala).

b_hedmork.first_mention_attestation: Historia Norwegiæ (c. 1170 CE) and Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE) as Heiðmǫrk / Heinafylki

morphemes.translation: heath, uncultivated land (or the Heinir people)

b_hedmork.etymology_analysis: Hedmork (Old Norse Heiðmǫrk, modern Hedmarken) combines heiðr ('heath, uncultivated land') or the tribal name Heinir with mǫrk ('forest, borderland').

b_valdres.first_mention_attestation: Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE) and other 12th–13th century CE kings' sagas as Valdres
b_valdres.etymology_analysis: Valdres (Old Norse Valdres) is an ancient valley name, plausibly reconstructed from *Vallres with an epenthetic -d-, combining vǫllr ('meadow, grassy plain') and *res (related to rás 'track, route'), meaning 'the route across/along the meadows'.

b_stange.first_mention_attestation: Hákonar saga Hákonarsonar (written c. 1265 CE, recording Stange Church in 1225 CE as Stangir)
b_stange.etymology_analysis: Named after the old Stange farm (Old Norse Stangir, plural of stǫng 'bar, pole, rod'), referring to the long ridge/hill on which the farm sits.

b_bothin.first_mention_attestation: Aslak Bolt's cadastre (1432–1433 CE) as Boðinjar syslo (Bodin Church built c. 1240 CE)
b_bothin.etymology_analysis: Bothin (modern Bodin) comes from Old Norse Boðin / Boðvin, likely combining boði ('skerry') and vin ('meadow, pasture').

b_rodoy.first_mention_attestation: Aslak Bolt's cadastre (1432–1433 CE) as Rauðeyjar halffylke
b_rodoy.etymology_analysis: Rodoy (modern Rødøy) derives from Old Norse Rauðey ('red island'), referring to the reddish color of the rocks on Rødøya.

b_aarborte.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Southern Sámi name for Hattfjelldal (parish formed 1859 CE, municipality 1862 CE)
b_aarborte.etymology_analysis: Aarborte is the Southern Sámi name for Hattfjelldal in interior Helgeland, Nordland. Historically inhabited by Sámi before Norwegian farming settlement in the mid-19th century CE, with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sandnes.first_mention_attestation: Egils saga (written c. 1230–1240 CE, describing Sandnesgården in the late 9th century CE)
b_sandnes.etymology_analysis: Sandnes (modern Sandnessjøen on Alsta) derives from Old Norse sandr ('sand') and nes ('headland'), meaning 'the sandy headland'.

b_utan_namdal.first_mention_attestation: Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE), Egils saga (c. 1230–1240 CE), and Frostathingslov as Naumudalr / Naumdælafylki
b_utan_namdal.etymology_analysis: Utan Namdal ('outer Namdalen', Ytre Namdal) combines the directional modifier útan ('outer') with Namdalen (Old Norse Naumudalr), named after the river Namsen (Old Norse Nauma).

b_innan_namdal.first_mention_attestation: Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE), Egils saga (c. 1230–1240 CE), and Frostathingslov as Naumudalr / Naumdælafylki
b_innan_namdal.etymology_analysis: Innan Namdal ('inner Namdalen', Indre Namdal) combines the directional modifier innan ('inner') with Namdalen (Old Norse Naumudalr), named after the river Namsen (Old Norse Nauma).

b_torgar.first_mention_attestation: Egils saga (c. 1230–1240 CE) and 12th–13th century CE kings' sagas (Viljalm of Torgar, d. 1139 CE)
b_torgar.etymology_analysis: Torgar (modern Torget on the island of Torget in Brønnøy) is the Old Norse plural of torg ('marketplace, public square'), reflecting its status as an aristocratic estate and trading/gathering centre in southern Hålogaland.

b_grong.first_mention_attestation: Reformatsen (1589 CE) as a parish under Overhalla (medieval Old Norse form reconstructed as Granungar)
b_grong.etymology_analysis: Grong probably derives from Old Norse Granungar, a collective/ethnonymic derivation from grǫn ('spruce'), referring to the people or settlement of the spruce-forested area in Namdalen.

b_vastvagborg.first_mention_attestation: 1963 CE (Vestvågøy Municipality formed; Borg chieftain hall is archaeological, while the island's medieval Old Norse name was Lófótr)
b_vastvagborg.etymology_analysis: Vastvagborg is a modern/game compound combining Vestvåg- ('west bay', from Vestvågøya, whose Old Norse name was Lófótr) with Borg (the Viking Age chieftain's seat on Vestvågøya).

b_bjarkoy.first_mention_attestation: Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE, describing Bjarkey / Bjarkarey as the seat of Þórir hundr c. 1030 CE)
b_bjarkoy.etymology_analysis: Bjarkoy (modern Bjarkøy) derives from Old Norse Bjarkarey ('birch island'), possibly also influenced as a trading-place name by Birka in Sweden.

b_vagan.first_mention_attestation: Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE) and Grettis saga (14th century CE, referring to 1012–1013 CE) as Vágar
b_vagan.etymology_analysis: Vagan (modern Vågan, historically Vágar) is the Old Norse plural of vágr ('bay, cove'), referring to the protected bays around Kabelvåg in Lofoten.

b_reydarfjall.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE Landnámabók (recording Reyðarfjörður in East Iceland; Reyðarfjall is a nearby peak)

morphemes.translation: rorqual whale / Arctic char (genitive singular of reyðr)

b_reydarfjall.etymology_analysis: Reyðarfjall is a mountain peak in Austurland near Reyðarfjörður (earlier Búðareyri), combining Old Norse/Icelandic reyðr ('whale/char') and fjall ('mountain'). Norse settlement of Iceland began around 870–874 CE.

b_hofn.first_mention_attestation: 1897 CE (founded as a trading post by Ottó Tuliníus, relocated from Papós)
b_hofn.etymology_analysis: Höfn (fully Höfn í Hornafirði) means 'harbour' in Icelandic (from Old Norse hǫfn). The town was founded in 1897 CE when a trading station established in 1861 CE at Papós was relocated to the site.

b_husavik.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE Landnámabók (describing Garðar Svavarsson wintering there c. 870 CE)
b_husavik.etymology_analysis: Húsavík means 'bay of houses' in Old Norse/Icelandic, referring according to Landnámabók to the winter houses built there by Swedish explorer Garðar Svavarsson around 870 CE.

b_vopnafjordur.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE Landnámabók and Vápnfirðinga saga as Vápnafjörður
b_vopnafjordur.etymology_analysis: Vopnafjörður (Old Norse Vápnafjörðr) means 'weapon fjord' (traditionally associated with Viking settler Eyvindr vápni). The fjord and settlement are attested in medieval Icelandic sagas and Landnámabók.

b_stokkseyri.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE Landnámabók (named for the high-seat pillars of settler Hásteinn Atlason after 874 CE)

morphemes.translation: of the high-seat pillar / log (genitive of stokkr)

b_stokkseyri.etymology_analysis: Stokkseyri means 'pillar sandbank', named according to Landnámabók because the high-seat pillars (setstokkar) cast overboard by settler Hásteinn Atlason washed ashore there.

b_klaustur.first_mention_attestation: 1186 CE (founding of Kirkjubæjarklaustur Benedictine convent by Bishop Þorlákur Þórhallsson)
b_klaustur.etymology_analysis: Klaustur (short for Kirkjubæjarklaustur, 'church-farm cloister') derives from the Benedictine nunnery founded at Kirkjubær in 1186 CE.

b_reykjavik.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century CE Íslendingabók (c. 1122–1133 CE) and Landnámabók (recording Ingólfr Arnarson settling Reykjavík c. 870–874 CE)
b_reykjavik.etymology_analysis: Reykjavík (originally Reykjarvík) means 'smoky bay' in Old Norse, named by Ingólfr Arnarson (c. 870–874 CE) after the steam rising from local geothermal hot springs.

b_vestfirdir.first_mention_attestation: 13th-century CE Icelandic sagas and Landnámabók (referring to Vestfirðingafjórðungr / Vestfirðir)
b_vestfirdir.etymology_analysis: Vestfirðir (the Westfjords) means 'west fjords' in Old Norse/Icelandic, designating the rugged northwestern peninsula of Iceland settled after 870 CE.

b_olafsvik.first_mention_attestation: 1687 CE (first town in Iceland granted a commercial charter by the King of Denmark on 14 April 1687 CE)
b_olafsvik.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 CE Norse-Icelandic settler or landowner named Óláfr (Old Norse Óláfr), whose bay (vík) it was.
b_olafsvik.etymology_analysis: Ólafsvík means 'Óláfr's bay', named after an Icelandic settler or landowner named Óláfr after the Norse settlement of Iceland (post-870 CE). It received Iceland's first commercial licence in 1687 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Borg â Mîrum (constituent holding of West-Îslant)

b_tanna.first_mention_attestation: 1406 CE deed of purchase as 'Tennanessi bøø' (Tännäs in Härjedalen)
b_tanna.etymology_analysis: Tanna (modern Tännäs) derives from Old Norse tenda ('the glittering/shining one', referring to the river Tännån) + nes ('headland'), first attested in 1406 CE as Tennanessi bøø.

b_storsjo.first_mention_attestation: 1482 CE written record as 'Stadsio' (Storsjö in Härjedalen)
b_storsjo.etymology_analysis: Storsjö (first attested 1482 CE as Stadsio) takes its name from Lake Storsjön in northwestern Härjedalen, meaning 'great lake'.

b_sveg.first_mention_attestation: 1270s CE medieval records mentioning Sveg as a thing-site (tingsplats)

morphemes.translation: bend, curve (referring to the bend in the river Ljusnan)

b_sveg.etymology_analysis: Sveg derives from Old Norse sveigr ('bend, curve'), referring to the sharp bend made by the river Ljusnan just below Sveg Church. It is attested as a thing-site from the 1270s CE.

b_helgum.first_mention_attestation: Late 15th century CE (Helgums socken formed c. 1480 CE; name attested in 1535 CE as Helghijöm)
b_helgum.etymology_analysis: Helgum (attested 1535 CE as Helghijöm) is a compound of helig ('holy') and hem ('homestead, farm'), or alternatively transferred from Helgum in Säbrå parish.

morphemes.translation: older name of the river Indalsälven

b_indal.etymology_analysis: Indal (first attested in 1344 CE) combines an older river name for Indalsälven with dal ('valley').

b_finnforsar.first_mention_attestation: 16th-century CE Swedish court records (1570/1574 CE regarding Finnforsen; Storfinnforsen on Faxälven in Ramsele, Ångermanland)
b_finnforsar.etymology_analysis: Finnforsar (referring to Finnforsen / Storfinnforsen on the Faxälven in Ramsele, Ångermanland) combines finn (historically denoting Sámi or Finns) with forsar ('rapids, waterfalls').

b_follinge.etymology_analysis: Föllinge (attested 1410 CE as Filinge, 1464 CE as Fölingom) derives from Lake Föllingesjön, interpreted as 'the lake with a plank-bridge/footbridge' (from fjäl 'plank, bridge' + -inge).

b_froso.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Norse/Swedish sources as Fræseyjar (12th–13th century CE; the c. 1050 CE Frösö Runestone stands on the island and mentions Jamtaland)
b_froso.eponym_details: Named after the Norse Vanir fertility god Freyr (Old Swedish Frö).
b_froso.etymology_analysis: Frösön (medieval Fræseyjar) means 'Freyr's island', named after the Norse god Freyr. Although archaeological remains and the Jamtamót assembly date back to the late 9th century CE, the island's name itself is first attested in High Medieval written sources.

b_graftavallen.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; early modern/modern summer pasture (fäbodvall) and ski settlement in Oviken, Jämtland

morphemes.translation: the summer pasture / meadow (definite form of vall)

b_graftavallen.etymology_analysis: Gräftåvallen is a summer pasture (fäbodvall) and modern ski resort in the Oviksfjällen mountains of Jämtland, named after the Storgräftån stream and the pasture (vall) beside it.

b_skalstugan.first_mention_attestation: 1602 CE royal decree by King Christian IV of Denmark-Norway ordering mountain cabins built along the Jämtland–Trøndelag route.
b_skalstugan.etymology_analysis: Swedish compound meaning 'the shelter cabin', referring to the mountain waystation established in 1602 CE by decree of King Christian IV on the medieval pilgrimage and trade route between Jämtland and Nidaros/Levanger.

b_ardda.first_mention_attestation: 12th century CE (late 1100s CE construction of Åre Old Church along the Nidaros pilgrimage route; 'Ardda' is an unattested game/orthographic variant of Åre/Åredalen).

morphemes.translation: oars, or possibly mountain peak / point (compare Arum)

b_ardda.etymology_analysis: Represents Åre / Åredalen in western Jämtland (with 'Ardda' as an unattested medievalized spelling). The name Åre (Old Swedish/Jamtish Arum) is attested from the 12th century CE via Åre Old Church and likely derives from a plural topographic or river/peak term.

b_krokar.first_mention_attestation: 1437 CE written attestation 'i Krokom' (dative plural of Old Norse krókr).
b_krokar.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse krókar (dative plural krókum, modern Swedish Krokom), meaning 'the bends' or 'the crooks', referring to bends along the Indalsälven river or shoreline.

b_morarna.first_mention_attestation: 1351 CE as 'Møresildræ' (Mörsil parish in Jämtland; 'Morarna' / Old Norse 'Mórar' is the plural topographic form).

morphemes.translation: moor, heath, or dense/boggy spruce forest

b_morarna.etymology_analysis: Swedish definite plural of 'mor' (Old Norse mór / mǿrr), denoting dense, damp spruce forest or level boggy woodland in Jämtland; the corresponding parish center Mörsil is first attested in 1351 CE as Møresildræ.

b_ostavall.first_mention_attestation: c. 1590 CE documented as 'Hofdavall' (new settlement; later Östavall in Haverö parish).
b_ostavall.etymology_analysis: Swedish compound meaning 'eastern meadow/field' (corresponding to Old Norse *eystrivöllr). Documented around 1590 CE as the new clearing Hofdavall before becoming Östavall.

b_ragunda.first_mention_attestation: 29 January 1290 CE as 'Rawnd' in a charter from Ragunda Church (Jämtlands och Härjedalens diplomatarium I:4).

morphemes.translation: ancient name of the widened lake/stretch of the Indalsälven river

b_ragunda.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Norse/Jamtish Ravund (attested as Rawnd in 1290 CE), originally the name of the former Lake Ragundasjön, a broad stretch of the Indalsälven river.

b_torshavn.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200 CE in Færeyinga saga ('þar er höfn sú er heitir í Þórshöfn'), describing Viking Age assemblies.
b_torshavn.eponym_details: Thor (Old Norse Þórr), the Norse god of thunder.
b_torshavn.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Þórshöfn ('Thor's harbour'), named after the Norse god Thor. Although Norse settlers established a ting at Tinganes in the 9th century CE, the name Tórshavn is first attested in Færeyinga saga (c. 1200 CE).

b_kirkwall.first_mention_attestation: Orkneyinga saga (written c. 1200 CE, recording events of 1046 CE) as 'Kirkjuvágr'.
b_kirkwall.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Kirkjuvágr ('church bay'), established by Norse settlers by the 11th century CE and anglicized via Scots 'Kirkwaa' to Kirkwall.

b_scalloway.first_mention_attestation: 1592 CE charter ('within the boundis of Scalloway', Melby Papers); 16th-century Hanseatic records also attest 'Schaldewage'.
b_scalloway.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Skálavágr ('bay of the hall' or 'bay of the huts'), evolving through Norn and Scots into Scalloway.

b_firdafylki.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Firðafylki'.

morphemes.translation: fjords; also the inhabitants of the fjords (genitive firða)

b_firdafylki.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Firðafylki ('county of the fjord-dwellers'), derived from firðir ('fjords', and its inhabitants) + fylki ('district/county').

b_jolster.first_mention_attestation: c. 1350 CE in Bergens Kalvskinn as 'Jǫlmstr' (medieval parish records of Bergen diocese).
b_jolster.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Jǫlmstr, derived from Proto-Norse *elmustru (related to Germanic *elma-, 'shining, white'), originally the name of the river Jølstra.

b_raumsdali.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Raumsdalr'.
b_raumsdali.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Raumsdalr ('valley of *Raumr'), derived from an uncompounded name for the Romsdalsfjord and the river Rauma.

b_northri_more.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Norðmœri'.

morphemes.translation: coastland or bogland (from marr, 'sea' or bog)

b_northri_more.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Norðmœri ('North Møre'), combining directional norðr ('north') with Mǿrr/Mœri (from Old Norse marr, 'sea' or 'wet/boggy coastland').

b_sunnmore.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Sunnmœri'.

morphemes.translation: coastland or bogland (from marr, 'sea' or bog)

b_sunnmore.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Sunnmœri ('South Møre'), combining sunn- ('south') with Mǿrr/Mœri ('coastland' or 'bogland').

b_nidaros.first_mention_attestation: 997 CE traditional foundation by Olav Tryggvason as recorded in Heimskringla (c. 1230 CE) as 'Niðaróss'.
b_nidaros.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Niðaróss ('mouth of the River Nid'), referring to the settlement's position where the Nidelva river empties into the Trondheimsfjord.

b_eynafylki.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200–1230 CE in the Frostating Law and Heimskringla as 'Eynafylki'.
b_eynafylki.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Eynafylki ('county of the Eynir'), named after the inhabitants (eynir) of the Inderøy peninsula ('inner island') in Innherred, Trøndelag.

b_verdala.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200–1230 CE in the Frostating Law and Heimskringla as 'Verdalr' / 'Verdœlafylki'.

morphemes.translation: from *Ver, old name of the Verdalselva river

b_verdala.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Verdalr (plural/genitive Verdala), combining an old river name (*Ver, meaning 'calm' or 'winding') with dalr ('valley').

b_hitrar.first_mention_attestation: c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla (Old Norse 'Hitr' / 'Hitrar') and 1432 CE in Aslak Bolts jordebok ('Hitr').

morphemes.translation: cleft, split, or indented island (plural Hitrar)

b_hitrar.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Hitr (plural Hitrar), an ancient island name meaning 'the cleft/split one' or 'the indented one', referring to the island's deeply indented coastline and bays.

b_bjorgvin.first_mention_attestation: 1070 CE traditional foundation of Bergen by King Olav Kyrre as 'Bjǫrgvin' (recorded in Heimskringla, c. 1230 CE).
b_bjorgvin.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Bjǫrgvin ('the green meadow among the mountains'), later shortened and adapted into Bergen.

b_northrihordalandi.first_mention_attestation: Late 12th century CE (c. 1190–1200 CE in medieval Norwegian sources dividing Hordaland into Norðhǫrðaland and Sunnhǫrðaland).
b_northrihordalandi.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Norðhǫrðaland ('northern land of the Hords'), a late 12th-century administrative division of Hǫrðaland.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (787/789 CE entry, 'Hæreðaland' / 'Hørthaland'); tribe earlier attested as 'Arochi' in Jordanes, Getica 3.24 (551 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Late 12th-century administrative subdivision of Hǫrðaland (attested 787/789 CE in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) with a post-867 directional prefix.

b_sunnhordalandi.first_mention_attestation: Late 12th century CE (c. 1190–1200 CE in medieval Norwegian sources dividing Hordaland into Norðhǫrðaland and Sunnhǫrðaland).
b_sunnhordalandi.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Sunnhǫrðaland ('southern land of the Hords'), a late 12th-century administrative division of Hǫrðaland.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (787/789 CE entry, 'Hæreðaland' / 'Hørthaland'); tribe earlier attested as 'Arochi' in Jordanes, Getica 3.24 (551 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Late 12th-century administrative subdivision of Hǫrðaland (attested 787/789 CE in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) with a post-867 directional prefix.

b_hardanger.first_mention_attestation: c. 1220–1230 CE in Fagrskinna and Heimskringla as 'Harðangr'.
b_hardanger.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Harðangr ('fjord of the Hords' or 'hard/stormy fjord'), originally the name of the Hardangerfjord before applying to the surrounding district.

b_voss.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200–1230 CE in Sverris saga and Heimskringla as 'Vǫrs'.
b_voss.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Vǫrs, probably originally the ancient name of Lake Vangsvatnet, derived from a root meaning 'water'.

b_jatharr.first_mention_attestation: c. 900 CE in skaldic verse (Haraldskvæði / Torf-Einarr, preserved in 13th-century sagas) as 'Jaðarr'.
b_jatharr.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Jaðarr ('edge, rim'), referring to the flat, 65 km coastal edge of southwestern Norway.

b_ryfylki.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Rygjafylki'.
b_ryfylki.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Rygjafylki ('county of the Rygir/Rugii'), referring to the Germanic tribe of the Rygir (Rugii) who inhabited Rogaland.

b_haugelandi.first_mention_attestation: c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla ('Haugar' / Karmsund area; 'Haugaland' as a regional name).
b_haugelandi.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Haugar ('the mounds') + land, originally denoting the district around the historic farm and burial mounds at Haugar (near modern Haugesund).

b_sognfylki.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Sygnafylki' / 'Sogn'.

morphemes.translation: people of Sogn (from Sogn, 'to suck', referring to tidal currents)

b_sognfylki.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Sygnafylki ('county of the Sygnir'), derived from the fjord name Sogn (from the root of súga, 'to suck', referring to strong tidal currents at the fjord mouth).

b_stolsheimen.first_mention_attestation: Modern Norwegian regional/hiking area name (Stølsheimen nature preserve established 1990 CE).
b_stolsheimen.etymology_analysis: Modern Norwegian compound meaning 'the realm of summer dairy farms' (støl + heimen), coined for the mountainous pasture region between Sognefjorden and Voss.

b_bremanger.first_mention_attestation: c. 1350 CE in Bergens Kalvskinn as 'Brimangr'.
b_bremanger.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Brimangr ('fjord where the sea breaks strongly'), combining brim ('surf') and angr ('fjord').

b_dale.first_mention_attestation: c. 1350 CE in Bergens Kalvskinn as 'Dalskirkue' (Dale in Sunnfjord / Fjaler).
b_dale.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Dalr (dative í Dali, 'in the valley'), referring to the valley settlement at the head of Dalsfjorden in Sunnfjord.

b_fjarlandi.first_mention_attestation: c. 1350 CE in Bergens Kalvskinn (medieval church/parish records of Fjærland in Sogn).
b_fjarlandi.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Fjǫrland / Fjærland, combining a form related to fjǫrðr ('fjord') with land ('land'), denoting the farming valley at the head of Fjærlandsfjorden.

b_bagahus.first_mention_attestation: 1308 CE construction of Bohus Fortress ('Bágahús' / 'Båhus') begun by King Haakon V Magnusson of Norway.

morphemes.translation: from Bagaholmen (the islet in the Göta älv)

b_bagahus.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Bágahús ('stronghold on Bagaholmen'), built in 1308 CE by King Haakon V Magnusson as Norway's southern border fortress; later gave its name to Bohuslän.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Kungahälla / Bohus (ancient Norwegian royal assembly and assembly seat) (in-game: Kuninghalle)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient Norwegian royal seat Kungahälla.

b_ranariki.first_mention_attestation: 551 CE in Jordanes's Getica (3.23–24) as 'Aeragnaricii' and 'Ranii'.
b_ranariki.eponym_details: Rán, the Old Norse sea goddess (traditionally cited in folklore, though philologists also link the name to rani 'snout/promontory' or raðr 'swift current').
b_ranariki.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Ránríki ('realm of the Ranii / Rán'), attested in 551 CE by Jordanes as Aeragnaricii / Ranii in Scandza, corresponding to northern Bohuslän.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ranariki (ancient district center of Ranrike) (in-game: Rânrîch)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient Iron Age district center of Ranrike.

b_telemark.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Þelamǫrk' / 'Þilamǫrk'.
b_telemark.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Þelamǫrk ('march/land of the Thelir'), named after the North Germanic tribe of the Þilir who inhabited Upper Telemark.

b_heddall.first_mention_attestation: 1315 CE indirect written reference to Heddal Stave Church ('Heitrardalr' / 'Hitterdal').

b_heddall.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Heitrardalr, combining an old river name (Heitr or Eitrá) with dalr ('valley'), later spelled Hitterdal before being standardized to Heddal in 1918 CE.

b_numedall.first_mention_attestation: c. 1200 CE in medieval Norwegian sagas and diplomas as 'Naumudalr'.

morphemes.translation: old name of the Numedalslågen river

b_numedall.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Naumudalr ('valley of the Nauma'), derived from the old river name Nauma (now Numedalslågen) + dalr ('valley').

b_tunsberg.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Túnsberg' (describing events c. 871 CE).

b_skiringssal.first_mention_attestation: c. 890 CE as Old English 'Sciringes heal' in Ohthere of Hålogaland's account in the Old English Orosius.

b_skiringssal.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Skíringssalr ('hall of the shining one' / Freyr's hall), attested c. 890 CE in Old English as Sciringes heal; associated with the Viking Age trading center at Kaupang and hall at Huseby.

b_drafn.first_mention_attestation: c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla (describing St. Olaf hiding in the fjord 'Drǫfn' / 'Drafn').
b_drafn.etymology_analysis: From Old Norse Drafn (fjord) / Drǫfn (river), derived from drǫfn ('wave'), originally the name of the inner Drammensfjord and Drammenselva before becoming modern Drammen.

b_ringariki.first_mention_attestation: c. 1170 CE in Historia Norwegiæ and c. 1230 CE in Heimskringla as 'Hringaríki'.

b_austfold.first_mention_attestation: 1543 CE first recorded attestation of 'Østfold' (replacing medieval Borgarsýsla).
b_austfold.etymology_analysis: Compound meaning 'the region east of the Fold' (the old name for the Oslofjord), first recorded in 1543 CE as an analog to Vestfold.

b_borgarsyslar.first_mention_attestation: Late 12th century CE (c. 1180–1200 CE under King Sverre's syssel division as 'Borgarsýsla'; named after Borg/Sarpsborg, founded 1016 CE).
